**The Tuner**

Marcus had been tuning pianos for thirty-one years, and in all that time he had learned one thing above all others: every piano is lying to you.

Not maliciously. Pianos don't have intentions. But a piano will tell you it's in tune when it isn't, tell you it's broken when it's only tired, tell you nothing at all while quietly falling apart in its own chest. His job, as he'd come to understand it, was not really to tune pianos. It was to conduct interviews.

He arrived at the Fenwick house on a Tuesday in October, carrying his case up the gravel drive the way he always did—handle in his right hand, case tilted slightly away from his hip so it wouldn't knock against him with each step. The case weighed eleven pounds empty and held everything he needed: tuning lever, mutes, felt strips, tuning fork, and a small flashlight with electrical tape wrapped around the handle where it had cracked in 1994.

Mrs. Fenwick met him at the door. She was maybe seventy, wearing a cardigan the color of oatmeal, and she apologized twice before he got his shoes off—once for the mess, once for the state of the piano.

"It hasn't been tuned in years," she said. "Since my husband passed, honestly. He was the player."

"I'll see what we've got," Marcus said, which was what he always said.

The piano was an upright, a Baldwin from the sixties, sitting against a wall in a room that smelled faintly of dust and lemon polish and something else underneath—old paper, maybe, or the ghost of cigarette smoke from decades ago. He opened the lid and looked inside the way a doctor looks at an X-ray. The strings were dull but intact. The hammers were grooved. There was a pencil resting on the frame, yellow, sharpened, with tooth marks near the eraser. He left it exactly where it was.

He pressed middle C. The note came out flat and slightly dead, like a voice answering a question it had been asked too many times.

He began at the bottom, the way he always did, stripping the felt across the strings and working upward note by note. This part of the job was almost silent—the mallet tapping, the lever turning in small increments, the test blows that settled the string into honesty. Outside, a leaf blower started up two houses away, and he paused until it stopped. Sound was the whole profession; you protected it jealously.

People thought tuning was about perfection. It wasn't. It was about compromise. Equal temperament, the system almost every piano uses, is built on a beautiful lie: you can't tune twelve notes so that every interval is pure. You have to spread the error around, distribute the imperfection so evenly that no single chord collapses under it. Every key becomes slightly wrong, and because they're all equally wrong, they all become usable. Marcus had explained this once to a client's daughter, a girl of about ten watching him work with her chin on her hands, and she had frowned and said, "So the whole piano is a little bit broken?"

"Exactly right," he'd said. "And that's why it works."

She hadn't seemed comforted. But she'd think about it later—he was sure of it. Certain ideas get into children the way splinters get into skin, invisible and then suddenly, years later, tender.

By the third octave, the Baldwin was beginning to open up. This was the part he loved, though he'd never say so aloud in a world that found piano tuning unremarkable: the moment when a neglected instrument starts remembering what it's supposed to sound like. The unisons lock in. The octaves stop howling. Chords that had sounded like arguments begin to sound like agreements. It wasn't music yet—a freshly tuned piano played badly still sounds bad—but it was potential again. Potential is most of what any of us have, if he was honest.

Mrs. Fenwick drifted in halfway through, stood in the doorway with her arms crossed over her cardigan, and watched without speaking. Some clients talked constantly. Some never said a word. You learned to read them the way you read the instrument.

"He used to play after dinner," she said finally. "Every night. Even terrible ones. Especially terrible ones, my mother would have said." She smiled at something private. "I haven't opened this lid since."

Marcus nodded slowly, keeping his hands moving. There was nothing to fix here except everything, and none of it was mechanical.

When he finished, he closed the lid gently and asked if she wanted him to play something. She shook her head. "It wouldn't be right," she said, "coming from anyone else today."

He understood. He packed his tools, wiped down the keys out of habit, and left the pencil where it lay. At the door, Mrs. Fenwick pressed a check into his hand and then, unexpectedly, held onto his wrist for a moment. Her grip was stronger than he expected.

"Will it hold?" she asked. "For a while?"

"Tuning holds as long as anything does," he said. "Come spring, it'll drift. They all do. That's not failure—that's just wood and wire doing what wood and wire do. You call me back and we start again."

She laughed then, a real laugh, brief and surprised out of her. "That sounds like advice."

"Everything sounds like advice if you've been doing it long enough," he said.

Driving home, windows cracked despite the cold, Marcus thought about the interview he'd conducted that afternoon—not with the piano but with the silence around it. Thirty-one years of rooms, of instruments holding their breath in corners, of people standing in doorways not knowing how to touch the things their dead had loved. The piano didn't need him, not really. It needed air in its strings and time under someone's hands. What the house needed was harder to deliver, and he delivered it anyway, the only way he knew: by making the thing true again, note by note, so that someday—maybe soon, maybe not—someone would sit down, press middle C, and hear it answer honestly for the first time in years.

That was the trade. That was the whole trade. And it was enough.
